It's well documented that Steve McQueen wore the Heuer Monaco (ref. 1133B) as Michael Delaney in Le Mans (1971), and it's one of the most famous film watch sightings. The cited source, a Watchonista article about Pedro Pascal, doesn't back this up, and the brand was just Heuer back then, before it became TAG Heuer.

Well documented: Pierce Brosnan's Bond wears the Omega Seamaster Professional Diver 300M Quartz (ref. 2541.80.00) in GoldenEye (1995). IMWDb and Omega's own history record it as Bond's first Seamaster.

Andy Warhol wearing a Cartier Tank is well documented. His line "I don't wear a Tank to tell the time" is widely cited, and his Tanks were sold at Sotheby's in 1988. The card's linked source, a Vogue piece about Timothée Chalamet, is off-topic and has no passages, but the sighting itself is real.

Sotheby's 2026 Space Exploration sale offered this LeCoultre 'Shark Deep Sea' ref. 2643 (circa 1970, cal. 72) as property from the Buzz Aldrin Family Trust, from his personal collection. Hodinkee, Gear Patrol and GQ also covered the lot. That proves he owned it, though I found no photo of him wearing it.

IMWDb, WatchPro, WatchPaper and A Timely Perspective all report that Michael Peña wears a Hamilton Khaki X-Wind Limited Edition as Rick Martinez in The Martian. Hamilton supplied the watch for the film, but no source gives the exact reference number.

Rolex's US site confirms the Datejust 36 ref. 126200 (m126200-0001, silver dial, Jubilee bracelet) at USD 8,350. It's a 36 mm automatic with 100 m water resistance, which converts to roughly the top of the CHF 6–7k budget. It's a classic everyday watch that suits a 15.7 cm wrist, and any specialist would gladly recommend it.

The Davosa Ternos is a well-regarded Swiss 40 mm, 200 m diver, and the quartz version is clean enough for the office. About USD 838 is roughly GBP 650, well inside the budget. I couldn't confirm this exact quartz reference on the distributor's site, but nothing I found contradicts the card's facts.

The specs check out: the WH1111 is a Swiss quartz steel 6000 that measures about 37–40 mm depending on how it's measured, so 39 mm is reasonable. But at USD 1150 it's poor value, since pre-owned examples usually sell for about USD 640–800, and the budget could buy a newer, better quartz or solar watch instead.

The Steinhart Ocean 44 is a well-regarded value diver with a 44 mm steel case, 300 m water resistance and a Swiss ETA 2824-2/SW200 automatic movement, so it fits a sport request under GBP 500. The approximate USD 580 (about GBP 460) is believable but sits near the top of the budget, and I couldn't confirm reference 103-1214 in my searches, though none of the other facts are contradicted.
The 130000C is the vintage Panthère 'Jumbo', and listings give its case as 29 mm wide (29 x 40 mm), not 36 mm. At 29 mm it is also too small for the 35–39 mm size the request asked for.

Oris's own page shows that reference 01 400 7790 4157-07 8 23 02PEB is the 43.5 mm Aquis Date Calibre 400 (USD 4,300), not the 41.5 mm model; the 41.5 mm version uses the 7769 case code. That makes the case size and model name on the card wrong, and 43.5 mm is outside the requested 40–43 mm range.

The card gets the model wrong. Seiko's own listing and retailer listings show the SRPL53 is the compact 'Slim Samurai' PADI Special Edition, a Samurai/Shogun-style case with a 4R35 movement and Hardlex crystal, not a King Turtle. The other facts are right: USD 650 retail, 41.7 mm, automatic and 200 m. The price, about £510, is also slightly over the £500 budget.

Bell & Ross's site and retailers confirm the specs: 42 mm, 300 m, automatic BR-CAL.302 movement, USD 4,600 retail. That price is roughly GBP 3.5k, so it fits the budget, and the 300 m rubber-strap diver suits a resort request and an 18.4 cm wrist well. Bell & Ross calls it 'Black Steel' rather than 'Black Matte', but the reference is the same watch.

The Eco-Drive One AR5000-50E is a 2.98 mm thick solar dress watch with sapphire crystal, sized at about 38–39 mm. That makes it a refined, distinctive office watch for a 15.3 cm wrist, and the approximate price of about USD 2.3k fits the EUR 2–3k budget. It may now be hard to find new, since Citizen Hong Kong's page lists it as unavailable, but the facts on the card check out.

TAG Heuer's official page and the aBlogtoWatch launch coverage both put this Carrera Tiger at 41 mm, not 39 mm, so it doesn't fit the 35–39 mm range for a 15.7 cm wrist (WatchBase's 39 mm figure looks like a database error). On value, it's a 300-piece limited edition with an ETA-based Calibre 5 that cost about USD 3,750–3,950 new, so roughly USD 7.2k pre-owned is poor value for this budget.

The card is accurate: the 1523.2 is a 36 mm steel-and-18k-gold quartz Classic, and dealers list it pre-owned for about USD 2,250–2,900, which sits inside the EUR 2k–3k budget. It's the original Hublot design, a slim 7 mm watch that suits an office and a 15.3 cm wrist, so it's an interesting vintage pick for an enthusiast. The gold and rubber-strap look won't suit everyone.

Maurice Lacroix's own site confirms every fact on the card: 42 mm steel case, ML115 automatic movement, 200 m water resistance and USD 2,950 retail, which is within the EUR 2–3k budget. It's a well-regarded integrated-bracelet sports watch that suits an 18.5 cm wrist for everyday wear. Its Sellita-based movement with 38 hours of power reserve is fairly basic for the price, but the finishing and bracelet make it a solid pick.

The facts check out: Aqua Terra 38 mm in steel and Sedna gold, self-winding calibre 8802, 150 m, discontinued, and about CHF 8,800 fits the budget. But the diamond dial on a burgundy leather strap is a dressy pick for a resort watch, and USD 11,013 looks high next to Chrono24 listings that run up to about $9,100, so a steel Aqua Terra on a bracelet would be a better choice.

Omega's US site confirms the facts: reference 220.10.38.20.09.001 is the 38 mm Aqua Terra Shades with a sandstone dial, rated to 150 m, at USD 7,400 retail, which is about CHF 6,000 and within budget. It's a versatile everyday watch in the right size for a 15.7 cm wrist, and a specialist would gladly recommend it.

Every fact on the card checks out: 41 mm case, quartz movement (L115), 300 m water resistance, and a blue dial. At about USD 681 pre-owned (roughly £540) it sits inside the £500–1k budget. A slim (10.2 mm) Swiss quartz diver from a respected brand like Longines suits the office brief well.

The Orient Kamasu (Mako III) RA-AA0006L19B is a blue-dial dive watch on a rubber strap. It has the F6922 automatic movement, a sapphire crystal, a 41.8 mm case and 200 m water resistance. At about USD 233, roughly £185, it's one of the best-value automatic divers well under the £500 budget.

The card links to the S301 bracelet version (S301-BK-BR), which Bremont lists at £3,500 ($4,000 in the US), not £3,100. £3,100 is the price of the strap version at Watches of Switzerland. Bremont has also retired the S301, so 'confirmed retail' is misleading. The 40 mm size, automatic movement and 300 m water resistance are correct.

The card's facts are right: 36 mm, automatic COSC movement, 100 m and ref. A37330531A1A1 are all confirmed, and USD 7,500 is about CHF 6k, inside the budget. But this is a diamond-bezel, mother-of-pearl dress-jewelry piece, not an obvious everyday enthusiast pick, and USD 7,500 pre-owned is poor value when comparable Galactics sell for about USD 5–5.4k and stronger everyday 36–39 mm watches fit this budget.

The specs are right: 40 mm Trip-Tick steel case, BE-92AE automatic chronometer and 100 m water resistance, and the reference matches how retailers list it (AIRCO-MACH-1/BK). Bremont has retired the model, though. List price was about $3,800–4,100, so the roughly $2,800 figure is a leftover-stock discount price, and a pilot watch on an ETA-based movement is only fair value against stronger options in this budget.
Chanel's own site lists reference H5699 as the J12 Caliber 12.2 in white ceramic with a 33 mm case. The card calls it the 38 mm Calibre 12.1, which is reference H5697 (black) and costs USD 8,350.

The specs are right: 38 mm steel and Sedna gold, silver dial, automatic Master Chronometer, 150 m, and the pre-owned price of about USD 11.2k (roughly CHF 9k) is in line with current dealer listings. It's discontinued, so you'd buy it pre-owned, but it's a classy resort watch that suits a 15.1 cm wrist and fits the budget.

I checked the details and they hold up. The reference is a real 41 mm quartz HydroConquest, water resistant to 300 m, and about USD 963 pre-owned (roughly £760) is within budget. It's a solid Swiss diver, but for the office a red bezel on a rubber strap is too sporty. The black-bezel version on a steel bracelet would suit office wear better.

The 36 mm case and quartz chronograph movement check out. But this is a discontinued older Conquest quartz chrono, and the same reference sells used on Chrono24 for about $700, so $1,364 is poor value in a budget that buys stronger current quartz or solar picks.

The model name on the card says "max bill Quartz 34mm", but ref. 041/4465.04 is the 38 mm max bill Quartz. The card's own 38 mm diameter field and dealer listings both confirm 38 mm. The USD 1,030 price, J645.33 quartz movement and 30 m water resistance check out, and the watch would otherwise be a good fit for this request.

The card says 40 mm, but Ingersoll's own listing (the card's source) and Selfridges both give the Grafton I00702 as 42 mm wide and 15 mm thick. That puts it outside the 37–40 mm range for this wrist. Even with the right size, it would be a weak pick: Ingersoll is a fashion brand, and a busy 42 mm multi-subdial design doesn't suit a simple office watch.

The 36 mm steel Defy Midnight with the Elite 670 automatic and 100 m water resistance fits the size, movement and water-resistance rules, and the pre-owned price comes to roughly CHF 6–7k. But its star-speckled, jewellery-style dial is a less natural everyday pick than options like a 38 mm Omega Aqua Terra or a Grand Seiko at this budget.

The facts check out: the reference is a 42 mm automatic chronograph rated to 100 m, and it lists at USD 2,645, with new ones from dealers at about EUR 2,080. A Swiss automatic chronograph with a 60-hour power reserve, at this price and in a size that fits an 18.5 cm wrist, is a solid everyday pick in this budget.
Reference 81925 is the Santos Ronde (also sold as the Santos Vendôme LM), a quartz model. Its case is about 32 mm, not 38 mm, so it falls below the 35–39 mm range the visitor asked for.

Bulova's official pages confirm the specs: 44 mm case, automatic movement (Miyota-based 821D) and 200 m water resistance. It's a well-liked revival of Bulova's own 1970s diver with sapphire crystal, and it fits this sporty request well. The approximate USD 488 is about GBP 385, which is plausible at discount sellers but below the roughly USD 795 that dealers ask. The model is discontinued, so it may be hard to find, and the movement is fairly basic.

The card says 600 m of water resistance, but the C60 Apex Limited Edition (2019, 100 pieces, 42 mm, SH21 in-house automatic) is rated to 300 m. It is also a sold-out limited edition that launched at £3,495, so it can realistically only be found pre-owned now.

I checked the card against IWC's site and dealer listings: the reference, 37 mm steel case, automatic calibre 32111, 50 m water resistance and price are all correct, and the price fits the budget. As a resort watch, though, a dressy diamond bezel on a leather strap is a weaker choice than a sportier 50 m+ watch on a bracelet. The USD 11,373 pre-owned price is also higher than new discounted offers of about USD 10,285, so the value isn't great.

The card's price is wrong. Borealis's own page for this exact no-date red-bezel version (BBSV2AD) lists USD 495, not about USD 375. Even at USD 495 (roughly GBP 390) it fits the budget, and the other facts check out: 38 mm, Miyota 9039 automatic, 300 m.

Grand Seiko's own spec page confirms everything on the card: 38 mm high-intensity titanium case, the self-winding Hi-Beat 9S85 movement, 100 m water resistance, a screw-down crown and USD 7,900 retail. That price is about CHF 6.3k, inside the budget. It's a well-finished, light everyday watch sized right for a 15.7 cm wrist. The only catch is the pink 'Sakura-Kakushi' dial, which won't suit every taste.

I checked the facts and they hold up: ref. 568.CM.1470.CM is the 38 mm all-ceramic Black Magic on a ceramic bracelet, with an automatic HUB1110 movement and 50 m water resistance. Dealer prices of about USD 11.1k–12.5k put it near the top of a CHF 9k–10k budget, and its black ceramic suits a resort setting. But the movement is a basic Sellita-based caliber, 50 m is the bare minimum for resort wear, and many enthusiasts don't rate Hublot highly, so a watch specialist would likely suggest better choices at this budget.

The Boldr Venture Field is a solid microbrand field watch. It's 38 mm, automatic and 200 m water resistant, all of which fit the request, and at about £260 it's well within budget. It's a tough everyday piece rather than a travel watch, though, so a GMT in the same price range would suit this request better.

All the card's facts check out: reference 220.10.38.20.03.004 is the 38 mm Summer Blue Aqua Terra in steel on a steel bracelet, with Omega's automatic calibre 8800, 150 m water resistance and a US retail price of $7,800. It fits the CHF budget and suits a 15.7 cm wrist, and it's one of the best everyday watches a specialist could suggest in this range.

The specs hold up: the B77346 is the two-tone steel and gold Windrider Callisto, about 34.4–35 mm, with a Breitling 77 quartz movement, and dealers list it at around USD 2,200–2,300. It's a solid quartz watch from a real watch brand, but a 2000s two-tone sports watch with a rotating dive-style bezel is an odd fit for the office, and it's pricey for an older quartz piece, so there are clearly better dress-leaning choices.

Longines' own page and several dealers list reference L4.755.4.11.6 as 'La Grande Classique de Longines', not 'Presence'. Présence is a separate Longines collection, so the card's model name mixes up two lines. The 36 mm size, quartz movement (L420), 30 m water resistance and about USD 1,350–1,400 price are all correct, and it would otherwise be a good slim everyday pick.

The W6700255 is the 36 mm steel quartz Ronde Solo de Cartier. That size suits a 15.8 cm wrist, and about USD 1.9k is a realistic pre-owned price within the budget. It's a well-regarded luxury quartz watch that a specialist would gladly suggest for daily wear when water resistance doesn't matter.

The Tsuyosa is a popular, good-value enthusiast automatic. It has a 40 mm case, a Miyota 8210 movement and 50 m water resistance, and its integrated-bracelet design works at the office. At about EUR 299 it sits well inside the CHF 500 budget, and the card's facts match the official listing.

The Santos Medium WSSA0010 is a steel automatic with a 35.1 mm case and 100 m water resistance, which matches the card. It suits a 15.7 cm wrist and everyday wear, and its quick-swap bracelet and strap make it a strong pick in this budget. One tracker lists retail at about USD 7,400 against the card's 7,250, but that's close enough that I didn't mark the price wrong.

The specs check out: 42 mm, Sellita SW200-1 automatic, 200 m and the reference. The KonTiki is a decent Swiss everyday watch that fits the request, but at about USD 2.8k for an off-the-shelf SW200 movement, the value is weak. Discounted copies often sell for much less, and Oris, Longines, Sinn or Tissot/Hamilton models with better movements are stronger picks at this budget.

Baume & Mercier's own page lists the Classima 10214 as a discontinued 'Heritage' piece that is no longer available, so 'USD 2900 (confirmed retail)' can't be a current retail price, and authorized dealers show it out of stock. It's also a dressy watch (silver guilloché dial on an alligator strap) rather than a strong everyday pick in this budget, though the 40 mm size, automatic movement and 50 m water resistance are correct.

Laco's official page and dealer listings give 20 ATM (200 m) water resistance, but the card says 100 m. The price ($2,220 retail), 43 mm case and automatic movement are correct, and the watch otherwise suits the request.

The specs check out: 41 mm, Swiss quartz (L157), 300 m water resistance, sapphire crystal and a steel bracelet. In the UK it lists at £850 RRP and sells for about £750, which fits the £500–1k budget. It's a smart, versatile sport watch that works well in the office, which makes it a strong pick for this request. The approximate USD 781 is a little under the $900 US list price but in line with what dealers charge (about $800–840).

I couldn't find a 'Flygraf Pilot M1 GMT' or reference YFLY22-GMT-BMS anywhere. Yema's real Flygraf GMTs (YAA21 references) are 39 mm, rated to 300 m and listed at USD 1,049–1,149, far over a GBP 500 budget, so the card's 40 mm, 100 m and USD 625 don't match any real model.

This fits the request: a real TAG Heuer diver with 300 m water resistance and a quartz movement, about 41–43 mm (listings disagree), at a price inside the budget. It's not a great office pick, though: the busy, sporty sailing-countdown dial doesn't suit dress wear, and the model is discontinued with a complex Calibre S movement that's harder to service. A plain Aquaracer quartz or a solar diver would suit better.

Rado's own page and the dealer listings show that reference R32150168 is the Captain Cook High-Tech Ceramic Skeleton (43 mm, R808 automatic), not the Diver, so the model on the card is wrong. Its size, movement and 300 m water resistance match the listings, and the EUR 4,500 price fits next to its CHF 3,950 and USD 4,700 retail prices.

The size, movement (Miyota 82S0 automatic), 50 m water resistance and EUR 340 price all match Laco's page for ref. 862103, the Aachen Blaue Stunde 39. But Laco lists this version as discontinued and no longer available, so it can't be bought at that price. The current bracelet version (862103.2.MB, EUR 440, in stock) would be the better card, and its sporty pilot style on a grey nylon strap is only a so-so fit for the office.

The facts check out: ref. 41034.02/S CA2C has a 43 mm case, an automatic movement (Sellita SW200-3) and 300 m water resistance, and EUR 3,770 matches dealers' pre-tax price of about EUR 3,170 plus VAT. It's a solid heritage diver that suits a resort, but 43 mm is the top of this wrist's range and the plain Sellita movement and weak resale value make it a lesser pick than options like a Tudor Black Bay 58 or Pelagos 39 at this budget.

The facts check out: the SSJ003J1 is a 39 mm Astron GPS Solar on Seiko's 3X22 solar quartz calibre, and it suits an everyday quartz-or-solar request in this size range well. The USD 1604 pre-owned price is a little high, since new ones have sold for about €1,180 on sale, but it is within budget.

Seiko's own site confirms the SSK023 at USD 450, with a 39.4 mm case, 100 m water resistance and an automatic GMT movement. That works out to roughly GBP 350, well under budget, and a true GMT at this size and price is a standout travel watch for a 16.5 cm wrist.

Timex's own listing confirms the facts: 44 mm, 200 m with a helium escape valve, a Miyota 8215 automatic, sapphire crystal and USD 499 on the bracelet (about £390, so within budget). It fits the request, but the basic 8215 is weak value at this price, and an Orient Kamasu, Citizen Promaster diver or Seiko diver would be a better buy for under £500.

The card's facts are wrong. Retailer listings and the card's own source page show reference 8086-4 is the LZ129 Hindenburg Solar chronograph, which runs on a Seiko VR42A solar quartz movement and has a 41 mm case. It is not a 40 mm automatic. Even if the facts were right, it would be a weak pick: Zeppelin is a fashion-leaning brand, and the watch's 50 m water resistance falls short of the 100 m you asked for travel.

The facts check out on Venezianico's own page: 40 mm steel case, Seiko NH35A automatic, 100 m water resistance and sapphire crystal. At €485 (about USD 550, roughly CHF 450) it fits the budget. It's a respected Italian microbrand, and this neat white-dial steel watch on a bracelet suits office wear and a 16.6 cm wrist.

The facts on the card check out: the Defy Midnight Borealis (16.9200.670/34.MI001) is a 36 mm steel automatic with 100 m water resistance, which suits a 15.1 cm wrist and a resort setting. But the diamond-set, blue-to-green dial is a dressy, women's-focused design rather than a typical resort piece. USD 11,212 is also expensive next to other pre-owned listings for the same reference at about USD 7,000–9,000.

Yema's official store lists the Flygraf Pilot M1 as 39 mm with 300 m water resistance, but the card says 40 mm and 100 m. The watch itself suits the request well: it has Yema's own YEMA2000 automatic movement and fits a 16.5 cm wrist.

The SBGX261 is a 37mm 9F quartz Heritage model rated to 100m, and Grand Seiko's US site confirms it retails for USD 2,700. That's roughly EUR 2.3–2.5k, inside the budget, and this is one of the best quartz dress or office watches a specialist could suggest for a 15.3 cm wrist.

I checked the facts with Omega and WatchBase: 42.2 mm, Co-Axial calibre 2500 automatic, 150 m and a white dial are all right, and the Aqua Terra suits resort wear well. But this is a 2003-era cal. 2500 model, and USD 4,000 is high next to listings around USD 2,900, so in this budget a newer pre-owned Aqua Terra with the 8500/8900 movement would be a better pick.

The specs check out: the 8926OB is a 40 mm automatic with an NH35 movement and 200 m water resistance, at about USD 135. But Invicta is a mall brand known for inflated list prices, and this is a generic copy of the Submariner. Enthusiasts have much better options under CHF 500, such as Seiko, Orient or Tissot.

Everything on the card checks out: it's the 5 Sports Field series, 39.4 mm, 4R36 automatic, 100 m water resistance, and Seiko USA lists it at USD 350. That's well under GBP 500. It's a tough, legible field watch that suits a 16.5 cm wrist and works well for travel. It has no GMT function, but an automatic GMT in 37–40 mm at this budget is rare.

All the card's facts check out: the SBGH343 is a 38mm 62GS in titanium with the 9S85 automatic Hi-Beat movement, 100 m water resistance and a USD 7,900 retail price, which comes to about CHF 6.3k and sits inside the budget. Its 44.7mm lug-to-lug, light titanium build and screw-down crown make it a strong everyday watch for a 15.7 cm wrist.

The facts check out: TAG Heuer lists WAR1113.FC6392 as a 39 mm Swiss quartz Carrera (officially the Carrera Special Edition) in black PVD steel, with 100 m water resistance. It suits the size and office brief, but a quartz Carrera at about $2,250 pre-owned is weak value at this budget, since sellers list it new for about that much. The black PVD finish on the case is also less versatile for the office than plain steel.

Omega's own spec page confirms every fact on the card: 35.5 mm steel case, the Omega 1680 thermocompensated quartz perpetual calendar movement, and 50 m water resistance. The pre-owned price is in line with dealer sales (one sold for £1,400), so it's a well-made everyday watch from a top brand that suits a 15.8 cm wrist and fits the budget.

Omega's site, the product sheet and dealer listings confirm the facts: the 1252.30.00 is a 35.5 mm steel-and-gold Constellation with the thermocompensated quartz perpetual calendar calibre 1680. Pre-owned prices of about USD 2,100–2,700 fit the EUR 2k–3k budget, and the high-accuracy quartz with a perpetual calendar, plus its dressy size, make it a strong office pick for a 15.3 cm wrist, though the two-tone full-bar style is a matter of taste.

The card calls this the Pro Diver GMT, but reference 9404 is a regular three-hand Pro Diver automatic with a white dial and an NH35A movement. It has no GMT hand, which matters for a travel request. The size (40 mm), automatic movement, water resistance (200 m) and price of about USD 91–106 are right.

The model name is wrong. Reference L3.830.4.52.6 is the 41 mm Conquest, not the Conquest 38. The 41 mm size, automatic L888 movement, 100 m water resistance and USD 2,400 retail are all correct, and the watch itself suits this request well.

The facts check out: TW2U29500 is the M79 Automatic with a 40 mm case, an automatic Miyota movement, 50 m water resistance and about USD 279 retail. But it's a 14.5 mm-thick diver with an acrylic crystal and a rotating bezel. That works as a casual watch, but office-focused picks in this budget, like the Orient Bambino or Seiko Presage, would suit the request better.

The GL0088 is a Combat Sub 42 with a 42 mm case, a Swiss automatic movement and 200 m water resistance, so every fact on the card checks out. At about USD 540 (roughly GBP 430) it's a sapphire-crystal Swiss sport diver that fits the GBP 500 budget, which is a strong-value pick for this request.

The card's model name is wrong. PY010C is sold as the Wave Master 300M, rated to 300 m, which even contradicts the card's own 300 m water-resistance figure. The 42 mm case, NH35A automatic movement and roughly USD 289 price are correct, and the watch itself is a well-regarded budget diver that would otherwise suit this request.

I checked the facts and they're right: a 41 mm quartz HydroConquest (L115) rated to 300 m with a sapphire crystal. At about USD 963 pre-owned (around GBP 760) it fits the budget, and it's a well-regarded Swiss diver that also works in the office, though the Arabic-numeral dial looks a bit sporty.

Ref. 140.019.5 is a small steel-and-gold quartz Reverso Lady from around 2000 that measures about 22 x 32 mm, not 37 mm. That puts it well below the 35–39 mm range. The quartz movement and the pre-owned price near USD 2.8k look plausible.

The watch is a good office pick, but the card says the case is 38.5 mm. Orient's official spec sheet lists RE-AU0002S at 38.7 mm, so the size is wrong. The approximate USD 497 also looks low next to listings from about USD 599, though an approximate price may vary.

The 37 mm case, 9F quartz movement and 100 m water resistance are right, and a Grand Seiko quartz is a great everyday pick for a 15.8 cm wrist. But the SBGX295 has a white dial, not black. The black-dial 37 mm Heritage quartz is the SBGX261, which retails for USD 2,700, above this budget. The SBGX295's USD 1,866 is close to what it sells for used, not its retail price.

This reference is the Classics Heart Beat Moonphase Date, which runs on the SW200-based FC-335 calibre, not an in-house 'Manufacture' movement. The official site and dealers list it at 40 mm (not 40.5 mm, so it sits just under the 40–43 mm range) and 60 m water resistance (not 50 m). The USD 2,895 retail price and automatic movement are correct.

The card's facts are right: the L3.759.4.76.5 is a 41 mm quartz Conquest (L157 movement) with 300 m water resistance, a silver dial and a brown leather strap. It's a dressy Swiss diver that suits an office and fits the budget, though at USD 911 pre-owned it costs more than its former USD 825 list price, so it's not a bargain.

The card's facts check out: this reference is a discontinued Longines Conquest with a 41mm case, a quartz movement, 300m water resistance and a silver dial on brown leather. About USD 729 pre-owned fits the GBP 500–1k budget, and the dressy sports look suits the office and the 40–43mm size range, though the leather strap is the weak point if you actually use the 300m rating.

Reference 126200-0023 is the Datejust 36 in steel with a domed bezel, mint green dial and Jubilee bracelet, as the card says. The 36 mm case, automatic movement and 100 m water resistance are all correct, and it fits a 15.1 cm wrist and a resort brief well. The pre-owned price of USD 11,166 (about CHF 9k) is within budget and realistic for this popular dial, though it's well above US retail of about $8,350.

Herbelin's own site says the Cap Camarat Diver models have 42 mm cases and use the 1745 reference series. The 1645 reference is the regular 40.5 mm Cap Camarat, which is only rated to 100 m, so the card's reference and 40.5 mm size don't match the 200 m diver.

The facts on the card check out. The US price of USD 5,200 is confirmed, and Breitling UK sells this reference for GBP 3,950, so it fits the budget. It's a capable 42 mm, 300 m sports watch for a resort trip, but at this price it uses an outsourced Caliber 17 movement, so the Tudor Black Bay or Pelagos is better value.

The specs fit the I.N.O.X. Chrono line: Swiss quartz, a 43 mm case and 200 m water resistance. The approximate price also fits under the budget, since steel siblings like 241983 and 241986 list at USD 800 and I couldn't find a separate listing for 241987. But this is a chunky, rugged, 13 mm thick sports chronograph, often sold on rubber, so it's a weak match for office wear. A sleeker 200 m quartz or solar diver or sports watch would suit better.

Baltic's own site confirms the facts: 38 mm stepped case, Miyota 8315 automatic movement, 50 m water resistance, from €385, which is inside the CHF 500 budget. It's a well-liked microbrand dress watch with a 1940s sector dial and a 47 mm lug-to-lug that suits a 16.6 cm wrist, so it's an excellent office pick at this price.

The specs on the card are correct: 43 mm, Powermatic 80 automatic, 300 m, and the reference matches. The approximate USD 568 is about what it sells for at grey-market dealers (its list price is USD 895), which puts it within a GBP 500 budget. It's a Swiss, ISO 6425-certified diver with an 80-hour power reserve, so a specialist would gladly recommend it at this price.

The card's facts check out: a 39 mm steel case, Kaliber 1 hand-wound movement, 50 m water resistance and USD 11,900 retail, which is roughly in the CHF 9–10k range. But it's a polished, hand-finished dress watch with an unusual time display, sold on leather or Alcantara, which makes it a poor fit for a resort watch that will see sun and pool water.

The card says the case is water resistant to 50 m, but Habring² and launch coverage rate the Chrono-Felix to only 30 m, which is below the 50 m the request asks for. The USD 10,979 price is also too high: retailers list the standard Chrono-Felix at about USD 8,350 (launch price EUR 6,250), and about USD 9,400–9,500 for special versions.

NOMOS's US store and Wempe both list ref. 782 at USD 5,050, not the USD 4,710 shown as confirmed retail. The other facts are right (42 mm, DUW 6101 automatic, 300 m), and it would otherwise be a strong resort pick.

The facts check out: L3.316.0.87.6 is the Longines Conquest V.H.P., a 36 mm steel quartz watch rated to 50 m. It's a good Swiss quartz watch in the right size and budget, but this ladies' version has a diamond bezel and mother-of-pearl dial that look more like jewelry than an office watch, and USD 3,198 pre-owned is poor value when discounted new ones are easy to find.

The facts look right: ref. Q1558421 is a 39 mm automatic steel triple-calendar moonphase with a meteorite dial and 50 m water resistance, and USD 11.5k pre-owned is about CHF 9.2k, inside the budget. But it's a delicate dress complication usually sold on an alligator strap, which is a poor match for a resort watch next to sportier picks in the same budget.

Oris's own spec and several dealer listings put the BC3 Day Date ref. 7500 at 40 mm, not the 38 mm on the card. They also rate it at 5 bar (50 m), which misses the visitor's 100 m minimum. The pre-owned price of about USD 599 (around £447) does fit the budget.

The facts check out: Ball's own site lists the DD3100A-S1C as 41.5 mm, automatic and 300 m water resistant, and USD 3,999 is about GBP 3,000, inside the budget. As a resort watch, this blue skindiver on a bracelet with tritium lighting suits the request well, though it is fairly thick at 14 mm.

The Citizen Promaster NY0040-09EE is a well-loved budget diver: a 42 mm case, an automatic Miyota/Citizen 8203 movement and ISO-rated 200 m water resistance. At roughly USD 244 it sits well inside the GBP 500 budget, and specialists often recommend it for this kind of sporty request.

The facts check out: the reference is correct, with a 42 mm case, an automatic Miyota 8215 movement and 300 m water resistance, and the price is well within budget. But it's a generic Submariner-style diver from a high-street jeweller brand, and Rotary has stopped selling it. A specialist would pick a Seiko, Orient Kamasu or Citizen Promaster diver at this price instead.

Grand Seiko's official spec pages list the SLGW003 as only splash resistant, not 100 m. That fails the 50 m minimum for this resort request, and its dress-watch build (crocodile strap) is a poor fit for resort wear. The price (USD 11,600), 38.6 mm case and manual 9SA4 movement are correct.

The Damasko DC56 is a well-made German tool chronograph with a Valjoux 7750 TOP automatic movement, a hardened steel case, 100 m water resistance and a 40 mm size. That makes it a strong everyday pick within EUR 2k–3k. The facts on the card match Damasko's specs, and the USD 3,094 price is roughly EUR 2,650–2,900, which sits inside the budget.

The card says 39 mm, but the linked source and other retailers list this Amphibia 120 case at 40 mm (14.5–15 mm thick). The rest checks out: the 2415.01 automatic, 200 m water resistance and a price around EUR 155 / USD 181. It's still a popular value pick, though as a bezel diver it's casual for office wear.

The facts are right: Zelos lists the Mako 300m GMT 'Frost' at USD 629, with a 40 mm case, 300 m water resistance and an automatic Miyota 9075 movement that sets the local hour hand on its own, which makes it a strong travel watch for a 16.5 cm wrist. But USD 629 is roughly £470–500 before UK import VAT and fees, so the landed cost likely goes over the £500 budget, and this limited edition may be hard to find.

A Seiko 5 Sports at about 40 mm with an automatic movement and 100 m water resistance fits the budget and wrist, and it's sound value. But the card names a whole product line with no reference, so the exact watch can't be identified. A sporty 5 Sports is also only a fair match for the office when dressier automatics in this budget exist.

Omega's own listing and Chrono24 confirm the facts: a 35 mm steel case, the Omega 1532 quartz movement, 100 m water resistance and the white Supernova dial on rubber. About $1,938 pre-owned is a believable dealer price within budget. It's a real Omega quartz that fits the wrist, but the diamond indexes, Supernova dial and white rubber strap make it a niche dressy piece usually sold as a women's watch, so plainer Constellation, Seamaster or Grand Seiko-type quartz options would suit everyday wear better.

The facts check out: the IWC Da Vinci SL Chronograph ref. 3728 is a 37 mm steel quartz chronograph with a JLC-based mecaquartz movement, and dealer listings are around USD 2,300–3,300, which fits the EUR 2–3k budget. It's a serious brand with a classic, slim office style that suits a 15.3 cm wrist, so a specialist would gladly recommend it, though at its age a service history matters.

The price on the card is wrong. Ball's official retail price for the steel-bracelet AeroGMT II is US$3,899, and dealers list this reference at about US$3,000–4,800 (EUR 4,359 at one European shop), so USD 2,681 doesn't reflect the real market and puts it above the EUR 3k budget. The 42 mm case, COSC automatic movement and 100 m water resistance are correct, and as a watch it would otherwise suit the request.
